title: Numbering the commandments
hook: Catholics and Lutherans number them one way, Orthodox and Reformed another; the words are the same

segments.voice: Yesterday, Augustine: love, and do what you will, with every act checked at the root. Your line was love decides. Which choice did love decide? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-three.

Ask a few Christians to recite the second commandment, and you may get two different answers, each said with total confidence. One says: no graven images. Another says: don't take the Lord's name in vain. Neither has misremembered. They grew up in churches that count differently. Catholics and Lutherans number the commandments one way. Orthodox and Reformed Christians number them another. The words on the tablets are the same words. Only the dividing lines move. Today: numbering the commandments, and why the Bible lets that happen.

Open Exodus 20 and look for the numbers. There aren't any. The passage runs from "I am the LORD thy God" to the warning about coveting your neighbor's house, wife, servants, ox and donkey, as one unbroken speech. What the Bible does give is the total. Later in Exodus, the tablets carry "the words of the covenant, the ten commandments." In the Hebrew, that phrase reads, literally, the ten words, which is today's line. So: ten. But where do the cuts go? Catholics and Lutherans, following a division tradition credits to Augustine, keep no other gods and no carved images together as the first word, then split coveting in two at the end: your neighbor's wife, then your neighbor's goods. Orthodox and Reformed Christians, and Anglicans with them, make images a word of its own and keep coveting together as the last. Jewish tradition counts another way again: its first word is God's own introduction, I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of Egypt. Each pattern underlines something. Setting images apart puts weight on how God is worshipped. Splitting coveting, some readers say, makes clear that a person is not a possession. Starting with I am says the law begins with who God is and what God has done, before any rule. Whichever way a church counts, every word is still read. The disagreement is about the dividing lines, not the commandments.

Here's the practice: read Exodus 20. Settle, and breathe. If you have a Bible or a phone nearby, open to Exodus chapter 20, the first seventeen verses, and read them slowly, once. Don't number anything. Just notice where you'd put the breaks, where one word ends and the next begins. If you don't have the text to hand, say the ones you remember, in whatever order they come, and notice which come to you first. The bell holds the time.
Numbering the commandments. The same ten words, divided in different places by different churches, with every word kept.

Your line: ten words. Today, pick one of the ten and watch for where it touches your day. And that's a week: from Taizé's repeated chant, through Iona, new monastics and prayer walks, to Augustine's love and the ten words. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: Christians learn the Ten Commandments in catechism, Sunday school and confirmation classes, and each tradition teaches its own numbering: Catholic and Lutheran catechisms one way, Orthodox, Reformed and Anglican teaching another.

notes: Numbering: Catholic and Lutheran (Augustinian) — 1 = no other gods + images, 9/10 = coveting wife / goods; Orthodox, Reformed and Anglican — images as 2nd, coveting as one 10th; Jewish — 1 = 'I am the LORD thy God' (Exodus 20:2). Confirm each, especially naming Anglicans with Orthodox and Reformed.

Exodus 34:28 Hebrew 'aseret ha-devarim' rendered 'ten words' (KJV margin and the Greek 'Decalogue' agree); the script states the Hebrew is 'ten words'. Confirm. The script avoids saying who writes on the tablets (34:28 is ambiguous).
'Splitting coveting... a person is not a possession' is attributed to 'some readers'; the Catholic split follows the order of Deuteronomy 5:21 (wife first). Confirm fair.
Jewish first word is paraphrased ('I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of Egypt'), not quoted.
Week-end carry looks back at days 1177–1183 by title (Taizé chant, Iona, new monastics, journaling and prayer walks); confirm if those scripts change.

Editor pass: 'following Augustine's reading' became 'a division tradition credits to Augustine' (historical attribution not in the cited text); 'everyone reads every word' and 'commas' line reworded to avoid an 'everyone' claim and a loose image.

Audit pass (2026-10-02): teach said 'in the Hebrew, that phrase is ten words', which reads as if the Hebrew phrase had ten words (it is two: aseret ha-devarim); now 'reads, literally, the ten words'. Numbering by tradition checked; no other changes.
